asr.full_text: These questions what's the difference between a xeon and a core i5 or core I7 processor. Is a xeon good for gaming they have been ask and answered a thousand times but the reason people keep asking is that there's a lot of misinformation in the answers that are floating around out there so let's address it here once and for all With the purchase of a qualifying Intel processor SSD or NUC You could instantly win an Intel gaming jersey and be entered in the draw for the ultimate system, click now to learn more Myth number one Zions and consumer CPUs don't work with the same motherboard So they're not not intercompatible This used to be true, when Xeons were actually made for completely different sockets But it's no longer the case Nowadays, it's up to the motherboard's manufacturer to implement support and in many cases it's possible to install a core i7 on a workstation board or a server board or a Xeon processor in a consumer board. But, certain CPU features, like overclocking on a workstation board, or ECC memory support on a consumer-grade board may not be validated. Myth number two, Xeons are inherently better for 3D rendering, and consumer CPUs like core i7's are inherently better for gaming. While in some cases, this will be valid, for example, this $2,500 12-core behemoth of a Xeon better for gaming. While in some cases this... will be valid. For example, this twenty five hundred dollar twelve core behemoth of a Xeon will not handle gaming as well as this three hundred and fifty dollar quad core Core i7. Because gaming favors fewer faster Cores compared to many slower ones. However, in cases where a Core i7 and a Xeon can be found based on the same microarchitecture with the same basic specifications, they should in theory perform exactly the same! But theories are just theories right? So i handed a Xeon E31276v3 and a Core i7 4790 non-k over to Luke, to find out if their performance other than support for ECC memory on the Xeon and a couple of consumer centric features on the core i7 is any different. And. They're pretty much same. You'll see the Xeon wins by very small amounts on average that's probably due to a bidding process more that anything. There's a bit of overlap for the bidding for i7s and Xeons and this could be a fairly high bandwidth Xeon and a fairly average I7. That's kind of about it. Very anticlimactic. Anyways, back to you Linus. Okay, so then why do Xeons exist at all? Well, for starters, they have ACC memory support which reduces the chances of a memory error occurring that can harm data integrity or system stability for mission-critical systems that cannot crash and along those lines, like other workstation and server grade components, they are indicated for 24-7 operation but that's not all. Even though we can find Xeons with the same specs as core series CPUs sometimes, the Xeon lineup also contains many additional products with specialized features that are not available to consumers usually because they simply don't need them. So why bother spending money on them? For starters along with that ECC memory support, some Xeons support massive amounts of memory per CPU and larger on chip data caches which will dramatically affect performance in certain workloads, especially very repetitive ones. There are also many Xeons available, Not only with additional processing cores for running lots of virtual machines on a single box, or for big performance boost in Workstation or server workloads, but as you move up the product stack, you'll find ones that can have two, four, or even more CPUs, in a single machine. For when a single, multi-core CPU still isn't enough. And then, finally, Xeon's being targeted at specialized customers like data centers, who are less concerned with the cost of a CPU, and more concerned with the higher cost of the rack space and electricity being used to support it over a long period of time they are available in configurations that are designed to deliver optimal performance per watt and per unit volume Compared to consumer chips where the assumption is most of the time there'll be the only CPU in the room anyway So in conclusion Xeons are different from core series processors But only if they are different for your workload it's not about which one is the best, it's about the right tool for the job so picking the wrong one won't make your PC explode so that's good to know but there is no need to pay a premium or give up consumer friendly features like overclocking to buy a Xeon if you are just going to edit videos on your PC from time to time However in cases where you need something not available to consumers it is also important to realize that consumer grade chips are just the tip of iceberg in terms of what's available out there. speaking of what's available out there do I ever have something awesome for you guys?
